content: Newcastle disease is a highly contagious disease that affects a wide range of domestic and wild bird species. It is particularly devastating in domestic poultry due to their high susceptibility, and outbreaks can have severe consequences for the poultry industry. The disease is endemic in many countries. Newcastle disease was first identified in the East Indies in 1926, but it was named after Newcastle-upon-Tyne, England, where it was rediscovered in 1927. The causative agent of the disease is the Newcastle disease virus (NDV), which is a negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus. It can also spread via contact with contaminated feed, water, equipment, or clothing. Humans who come into contact with infected birds, such as workers in poultry processing plants, may develop mild conjunctivitis or flu-like symptoms. However, NDV does not pose a significant health risk to humans. Interestingly, NDV has shown potential as an anticancer agent due to its ability to selectively destroy human tumor cells while causing minimal harm to normal cells. The clinical signs of Newcastle disease vary widely depending on factors such as the strain of the virus, as well as the health, age, and species of the affected bird. Symptoms may include respiratory issues such as gasping and coughing, neurological signs like depression, loss of appetite, drooping wings, and paralysis, as well as swelling of the eyes and neck. Other signs include diarrhea, misshapen or abnormally thin-shelled eggs, and a reduction in egg production. NDV strains are classified into three categories based on their virulence. Velogenic strains are highly virulent, causing severe respiratory and neurological symptoms, rapid spread, and mortality rates of up to 90%. Mesogenic strains are of intermediate virulence, leading to coughing, reduced egg quality and production, and mortality rates of up to 10%. Lentogenic strains are non-virulent, causing mild symptoms with negligible mortality. In 1999, researchers observed promising results when using the Newcastle disease virus in cancer patients. By 2006, scientists at the Hebrew University successfully isolated a variant of the virus, known as NDV-HUJ, which was specifically designed to target cancer cells. NDV-HUJ is a naturally occurring, attenuated (weakened) variant of the virus that preferentially infects and replicates in certain types of tumor cells, such as those in the brain and lungs, while sparing normal cells. This virotherapy was tested on 14 patients with glioblastoma multiforme, a highly aggressive brain tumor, and yielded encouraging results.
